Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Cold Temperature: Cold, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Nalani had always been a pillar of strength for her family. As a project manager at a large corporation and a devoted wife, she took pride in being able to juggle multiple responsibilities with ease. But everything changed when she was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness that required her to undergo months of grueling treatment. The memory of those hospital days still felt surreal to Nalani. She recalled the antiseptic smell that clung to every surface, the beeping of machines, and the cold temperatures that seemed to seep into her bones. But what happened during those long hours was fragmented - some moments crystal clear, others completely blank. She remembered the pain and fear, but not always in tandem with specific images or events. Sometimes, she'd find herself overwhelmed by emotions without any clear memory of why. As Nalani began to recover physically, she became increasingly consumed by thoughts of her own mortality. The medical equipment that had once saved her life now seemed menacing - the sight of needles and drips making her heart racing. She started avoiding hospitals and even refused physical examinations, fearing they would uncover some new, terrible truth about her body. At home, Nalani's avoidance habits took on a life of their own. She'd steer clear of any room that was too cold, cranking up the thermostat to an almost unbearable level just to avoid feeling that familiar chill. And when cooking or cleaning, she'd find herself suddenly overcome with anxiety if she caught a whiff of something antiseptic - as if her brain had linked certain smells directly to the terror of those hospital days. Nalani's inner world was in turmoil. She felt like she was constantly monitoring her own thoughts for signs of "going crazy," afraid that one wrong move would plunge her back into the abyss. To cope, she'd try to erase memories of the illness altogether - a futile effort, since fragments kept resurfacing at unexpected moments. The impact on Nalani's life was profound. She began to withdraw from social events and stopped taking care of herself physically. Her work suffered as well; simple tasks that once came easily now seemed insurmountable. As she felt her sense of control slipping away, Nalani became convinced that the trauma had destroyed not only her body but also her very identity. "I've failed as a wife," she'd tell herself, "I'm no longer the strong one." The thought sent her spiraling into despair - after all, hadn't she always defined herself by her ability to care for others? And now, it seemed like that was gone forever. Nalani's physical vulnerability haunted her every waking moment. She felt like her body had been irrevocably damaged, leaving her a shadow of her former self. As the months went by, Nalani became increasingly isolated - too afraid to leave the house or engage with friends and family for fear of being overwhelmed. It wasn't until she found herself unable to attend her own sister's wedding that Nalani realized she needed help. The event was a painful reminder of all the things she'd been avoiding - hospitals, ambulances, physical examinations... and life itself. As she finally sought out therapy, Nalani couldn't shake off the fear that had taken hold: would she ever be able to reclaim her life, or would the trauma forever define her?
